speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM FOR SUPPLYING OF BEEF, 1944-45-FLOOR PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that negotiations have been completed for a contract to supply the United Kingdom with a minimum quantity of one hundred million pounds of beef during the two-year period 1944 and 1945, and in addition to this minimum quantity all further surpluses of beef as they become available. The negotiation of this contract has the effect of assuring floor prices for beef on a revised scale.
In the case of special "Red Brand" beef and commercial beef of "Blue Brand" quality, the meat board will purchase for export to the United Kingdom an agreed quantity at prices 25 cents below their respective ceilings. If further surplus quantities of "Red" and "Blue" brand beef are offered to the meat
board, the board will purchase all such additional quantities at prices 50 cents below the ceiling.
Other qualities of beef will be purchased on the following basis: Choice and good quality cows, 75 cents below the ceiling; commercial quality not qualifying for "Blue" brand, $1.25 below the ceiling.
Accumulations of beef of lower qualities will be avoided by inclusion in the exports of substantial quantities of boneless manufacturing beef.
The above prices constitute in effect floor prices since the meat board will be prepared to buy all quantities offered to it.
If present trends of marketings continue and if high quality cattle come to market in an orderly manner, it is expected that the minimum quantities provided for in the United Kingdom contract will maintain the prices of "Red" and "Blue" brand beef at a point not lower than 25 cents below the ceiling. In any case, however, no matter how heavy or irregular the marketings may be, the producers of "Red" and "Blue" brand beef will have the complete assurance of the protection of floor prices at not less than 50 cents below the ceiling.
These new floor price arrangements will come into effect on August 21, 1944, and will replace the variable and graduated floors which have been in effect during the 1943-44 season. Under last year's arrangements, the floor prices ranged from $2.25 below the ceiling during the late summer and autumn months to 25 cents below the ceiling in the late spring and early summer months. The new floor prices will remain level throughout the year.

I hate to be considered to be even half out of order; I want to obey the regulations of parliament and adhere to the rules in all cases; but I believe this is the proper -time to bring up the subject which is in my mind, namely the investigation of a scientist-some doctors would not call him a scientist-a research worker who has given the best part of his years in research work endeavouring to find a cure for cancer. The man I have in mind is Doctor J. R. Davidson, of 232 Somerset block, Winnipeg. I hope that is definite. You have the subject of the remarks I am now going to make. I hope I am not going to be too long; certainly I do not wish them to be controversial, but if it should happen that they are, I shall try to uphold my end.

We have heard nothing with regard to the government's attitude; and because it is so vital to me I have taken it upon my shoulders to acquaint the people of Canada with the true situation, and 10,000 pamphlets have gone out throughout this dominion. To how many will it be news that similar conditions prevail in Canada? This is the truth, and it is a truth much more harmful than merely hateful. It may mean unnecessary sickness and premature death for very many among us-perhaps you or me, or one of our children or more. Much is very wrong right here, and right now, even in Canada, even in Ontario. I write, of course, as a layman; not as a technical expert in any field . . . experts, by the way, are often wrong, and sometimes silly; it is for you and me to use them, not to be ruled by them; to weigh them against each other; to be, as democrats, their masters, not their slaves.
In a succeeding article the same writer deals with the Davidson cancer treatment at Winnipeg, and he draws to the attention of his readers the fact that the Kiwanis club of Winnipeg saw fit to appropriate $2,500 to help Doctor Davidson in his research work. He tells of a mass meeting held at Portage la Prairie, and about a resolution passed there asking for a full and fair investigation into Doctor Davidson's work. Evidently this writer, of whom I know nothing, is imbued with the suspicion, if not belief, that a monopoly does exist in the medical profession. I want to submit some evidence which I also submitted at Portage la Prairie. May I tell you that when the committee was sitting on social security-I refer to No. 22,' held on Wednesday, June 16, 1943-the medical committee of the research council was represented by Surgeon Commander C. H. Rest, the opening paragraph of whose statement reads- and listen to this evidence, because it should be irrefutable:
Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen: The associate committee on medical research, of the national research council, wish to lay before the special committee on social security of the House of Commons, evidence that the national research council should be entrusted with the direction of any medical research program which
fMr. McGeer.]
will spring from the application of a national health insurance act.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is sufficient evidence. Now I want to say something in reference to what I said the other day. I am quoted in the Journal as saying that the member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) is mentioned as a possible minister of this new department of health which we are creating. That is all they say about it. If they had printed all my remarks I would not have said anything about it here. With all due respect to the hon. member for Renfrew South, I wish to say that if I were making the choice of a minister for this new department of national health, he would not be the one I woujd choose. If I were to make the choice-I do not think the government will grant me that privilege-I would choose a minister from the hon. members sitting nearer to me than the hon. member for Renfrew South. I just want to say that by the way. I have no fault to find with the newspapers, but sometimes they print these little articles which do not tell the whole story. This particular article seems to imply that I would support the hon. member for Renfrew South as minister of national health. I just want to make it plain to my hon. friend the member for Renfrew South and to all hon. members that he has not my support as a possible minister for this department.

speechtext: Does the hon. member confine himself to medical men? He speaks of those sitting nearer him. Have any of the rest of us any consideration in the matter at all, or is it confined merely to medical men?

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I let it go at that. The hon. member may have his hopes aroused, as other hon. members all over the house.
What I am about to say is said with all due respect to the hon. member for Renfrew South. He has not exhibited any desire to have Doctor Davidson's work further investigated. When this bill was before the house a while ago he said he thought that the federal government, the department of health and the national research council had gone far enough. Speaking personally he said he did not think the situation warranted the federal government or t'he national research council or the department of health spending the taxpayers' money in making further investigations. Then yesterday he said this, or words to this effect-I am not quoting, but hon. members can look it up in Hansard and see if I am wrong. If I am I expect I shall be called to order. He protested against the taxpayer deducting from his taxable income

Department of Health and Welfare
the medical fees he had paid outside of Canada. If that is not a tendency to a monopoly I do not know what it is. In fact one of the hon. members on the other side said that coming from the Liberal party, who he believed were more or less free traders, it was really illuminating. It was asking for a tariff for a certain profession.
I wish to suggest to the government that they cooperate, as this bill intends, with the provinces; cooperate by giving a grant to every province in the dominion to help them to set up some kind of clinic that can look into Doctor Davidson's work. That can be done and should be done in every province.
I mentioned a gentleman who telephoned me from Windsor, Ontario. I do not think that he would get near Doctor Davidson's office, because hundreds are being turned away from all parts of Canada, and some from the United States. You can understand that only a few of the people of Canada will have the privilege of coming in contact with the doctor. Therefore if t'he government is anxious and willing to exploit this possible cure it should help the provinces to set up these clinics in at least every capital city of the dominion. That is something I proposed before. I am deeply conscious of the fact that the Prime Minister is sympathetic, as are all hon. members of this committee, -but for God's sake let us have action. Approximately fourteen thousand people have died from cancer since I brought up this matter one year ago. The people are expecting action. That is all I have to say on this very important matter.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have heard it said that a drowning man grasps at a straw. For many long years the disease of cancer was considered, and it is still considered, largely hopeless. We never cure cancer; we cut it away, and if we cut away enough good tissue with the cancer sometimes we cut the disease away entirely and we get relief. More recently they burn it away with radium and X-ray. Fortunately the radium and the X-ray have a predilection for the diseased tissue rather than sound tissue, and sometimes the individual survives the application of radium and the X-ray, but it does not always cure cancer
There is a lot of ambiguity and misunderstanding with regard to the Davidson affair.
I will not even go so far as to call it "the Davidson cure for cancer"; but I would like to tell the story about Doctor Davidson, because I know it. I do not know whether the committee is interested in knowing about this little man, but I know about him personally and I can tell you about him. I have been talking to him personally and compara-
100-306J
tively recently, and I know most of the facts in connection with this case. Thirty-five or forty years ago Doctor Davidson was a leading doctor in the city of Winnipeg and has been ever since. He was on the staffs of two or three hospitals there. He was a trusted and leading man, and he still is a trusted and leading physician, although he is an old man now. As the attendant on the staff of the Winnipeg general hospital he had frequent cause to observe cases of new growths, cancer and sarcoma that entered the wards in a hopeless condition. In the ordinary course of his treatment in this hospital he had discovered cases that when they were fed on abundant full nutritional vitamin diet the disease was retarded or slowed up. So definite was this fact that he decided to work on it and to follow it up. At that time there was in the city of Winnipeg a prominent, outstanding surgeon by the name of Doctor J. E. Lehmann, who has since died. I got this story directly from Doctor Davidson's lips, and I think it is well that the committee should know it. A case came into the wards of the general hospital. That case was saturated with cancer that was called carcinomatosis, little cancer deposits growing in the skin of the arm, the shoulders, the scalp and the abdomen. She was full of cancer. She had been an operative case of Doctor Lehmann, and he also was an attendant of the surgical wards. When she dropped into the public ward, apparently to die, Davidson called Lehmann in in consultation to see his former patient. Lehmann said: "There is nothing you can do for the woman, Davidson. You may as well send her home to die." You see, hospitals do not like to have people dying in them. That is not what they are for. Hospitals are for curing people. Lehmann advised that the woman be sent home to die. Davidson kept her there for two or three weeks and he treated her with his idea of a high nutritional diet. Let me tell you what it is. It is chick embryos that have been incubated for thirty-six hours. He takes the fresh egg and he incubates it for thirty-six hours, and then he takes the chick embryo, the beginning of a new life and feeds them to the patient. Thirty-six of those embryos were fed to that woman every day for three weeks-not for three weeks all the time-while she was in the hospital. She appeared to recover, pick up strength and improve. She was sent home, and good word came back to the doctor from her at home. After eight months she came back to the hospital and presented herself to Doctor Davidson. He saw her, and behold, the carcinomatosis had disappeared, the little lumps of cancer in the abdomen, on her arms,

Department oj Health and Welfare
her back, her head and so on, and the lumps in her integument had apparently largely disappeared.
I know that there are a lot of sceptical men who would laugh at that. I would just as soon take Davidson's word as anybody else's. He called in Lehmann to look at the woman and he said, "I thought you were dead." She said, "No, I am very much alive, thank you." Lehmann said to Davidson, "I think you have got something; you had better go ahead and work on it."
That was the beginning of experimentation with rodents. Doctor Davidson has definitely established two principles. He has definitely established that he can retard the advance of cancer by a high nutrition diet. That is something definite; that is a principle. Let me explain the experimentation with rodents. They take a mouse and shave the hair from the back of its neck. Then they put a little spot of tar on the shaven place, and the mouse scratches away at that tar until he causes an ulcerating sore, which eventually becomes cancerous. As I told this house previously, Doctor Davidson experimented with two families of mice, one on ordinary nutrition and the other on high nutrition. He discovered that the mice fed on the high nutrition diet did not develop cancer after they had tar put on the back of their necks. Then he went a step further; he decided to experiment with the serum of the healthy families of mice, on the unhealthy families of mice, and actually discovered that when the unhealthy families of mice were injected with the serum from the healthy families, their cancerous sores cleared up. So that another principle was established. Those two principles cannot be denied by the research council of Canada or anyone else, because they have been definitely proven and shown.
Before leaving that point, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has recited in this house the testimony of a great many people concerned with this matter. The other day I received a letter from a lady whom I do not know, who is not a patient of Doctor Davidson, and who is not known to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. She is a Mrs. Florence N. Farwell, of Toronto, and she says:
In the last issue of Diet Digest an article appeared on cancer written by Dysen Carter telling of Doctor Davidson's work on cancer.
I think I can be of help, as my sister developed cancer and went right back to natural foods. It took us eight years to conquer the disease, but we did it. I am enclosing an article which will tell you a little of our struggles during those eight years, that is if you are interested in one's experiences and researches of her own life.

On another page I have a statement from this woman, who claims to be the sister of two doctors and who was told by her medical adviser that there was nothing for her but an operation. She decided against that, preferring death, and proceeded to give herself treatment by nutrition and diet. That woman is now living and well. Let me read just one paragraph from her letter:
When I developed cancer the doctor said it was a carcenoma cutis. As I did not know what he meant I looked in the medical dictionary and found the meaning of carcenoma cutis to be "a malignant cancer." I was stunned. Where could I turn for health? The doctors here said "operation", but I could not bring myself to consider that form of treatment, and my own doctor brothers said, "to leave it alone and live quietly and you may live a few more years." I told them that I could not sit quietly by and let it eat my life away, so, taking my life in my own hands, my sister and I went to work.
I am not going to read the rest of the letter, but it was in 1920 that she was told she could not live more than two years. This is 1944; she is still alive, and has done nothing but follow a strict diet. Apparently she has cured herself of what would seem to have been cancer; at least her brothers were ready to believe that it was cancer, and her medical adviser stated it was cancer. Here we have another instance along the same line as Doctor Davidson's idea, indicating that a high nutritional diet with abundant vitamins is antagonistic to the development of cancer. All right; let us go that far. If we have not actually established those two principles at least we have had them brought prominently to the attention of the people at large, so for God's sake let them hang on to them. As I said a moment ago, a dying man grasps at a straw. If there is anything at all in it; if there is anything to be followed up, let us follow it up.
But what are we doing? What investigation have we had? There has been none. I believe a Doctor Meltzer and a Doctor Campbell, both of Manitoba, were delegated by the Manitoba medical association or the Winnipeg medical society to investigate Doctor Davidson's cancer experiments. They followed up some of the earlier experiments with mice, and reported that they thought there was a good deal of merit in Doctor Davidson's work, but they could not substantiate his findings. That was their report, and there has been no investigation since. With all due respect to. the national research council I know they did not investigate Doctor Davidson's work, because I have been talking to Doctor Davidson about the matter and no one spoke to him personally about his work. They did send him a questionnaire: what did you do about this,

Department oj Health and Welfare
what did you do about that, and so on, a matter of some ten or fifteen questions. Doctor . Davidson answered a few of the questions but he said there were a few he could not answer because he was not able to keep the data, and perhaps was not sufficiently versed in the sort of information they required. An investigation of that kind is not what we want. Here we have the testimony of fifteen or twenty people who declare that they have been benefited- some say they have been cured-by Doctor Davidson's treatment of cancer. I will bet you there are hundreds of people with cancer all over Canada who would jump at the chance to be given that treatment. Why, we should establish small depots in hospitals here and there all over the country and get all people afflicted with cancer to come along and be treated in this way; I will bet there would not be a square inch to spare in any such clinics that might be established.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I hope I have not bored you to death or needlessly taken up the time of the committee, but for heaven's sake let us take some decent action in regard to this matter, so that we may relieve people dying of cancer. That is all I have to say.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, you have heard from a farmer and from a student of medical science. Now you will hear just a brief word from a student of the queen of sciences, theology. I think that will give you a good cross-section of the intelligence of this house. We do not want to find fault with the research council or to hurt any individual. 1 introduced this matter in the house a year ago, and all we ask is that the findings of Doctor Davidson be preserved. I do not care whether that is done by a committee of the research council or by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, whom I trust absolutely. Let us make some progress, that is the point. Doctor Davidson is one of the finest doctors in greater Winnipeg. I am sure he knows his stuff, to put it in everyday English. There is no sham about him.. We must see that his findings are preserved and handed down, for Doctor Davidson is over seventy, and he is not as young as some of us who are around that age. I am sure the Prime Minister and particularly the Minister of Pensions and National Health will not allow this matter to be ignored very much longer.
Mr. MeNEVTN: Would the Chairman permit me to ask a question which may be answered either by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie or the hon. member for St. Boniface? What assistance, if any, has been given by the government of Manitoba, through its department of health, in connection with this matter, which I recognize as all-important?

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: If that question is put to me, so far as I know Doctor Davidson has had no assistance from the government of Manitoba.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: I might reply to the hon. member by saying that at one time the government of Manitoba did expect the dominion government to make a grant in order that the medical faculty of the university of Manitoba might undertake an investigation. That investigation was not to be a sham. It was to cost money, because they were going to summon witnesses. It was the intention to call people who had taken treatment from Doctor Davidson and had been helped or cured, and to call other patients who had not been helped. It was going to take some money, but they expected to get this grant and they were prepared to go on with the work. The premier of Manitoba, with that in mind, said that it would not be within their responsibility to make a grant until this investigation had taken place. But the investigation has not taken place. I want to say in the shortest possible way that I do not think any action is going to be taken. I hope I may be pleasantly surprised and find that I am wrong in that assumption. If this government fails and if the Manitoba government fails, they will have to answer to the people; I am sure of that.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad that certain members of this committee are ready to lead a discussion on the question of cancer cure. I can give my whole-hearted support to that. Our endeavour should be to see that the people of Canada are given the results of any investigation that can be carried on in this direction. What I intended to speak about this afternoon was in continuation of what I said a little while ago when this bill was under discussion and when I supported the general principle. I mentioned at that time that in my opinion it was a great pity that section 5 of the bill did not state definitely in one of its subsections that there would be in this new department a group of officials whose sole duty would be to care for the health and welfare of children. Of course the Prime Minister, who is sponsoring this bill, will say that under the general provisions of section 5 the health of children would automatically be cared for. I must insist that child welfare is a specialized subject and should be dealt with by specially qualified officials who would devote their time to that service alone.
I do not think any hon. member of this house will disagree with me when I say that in war time the nation's best and first care should and does go to the armed forces. Our slogan is everything for the fighting front and

Department oj Health and Welfare
for the men who fight, and rightly so. Can we ever forget that during the last war we lost around 60,000 of our men, who were killed in battle, in four years of war, but that during four years after the last war we lost no less than
70.000	of our children, who died before they were a year old.
Upon different occasions and at different times hon. members of this house have risen to urge that the natural resources of Canada shall not be wasted, that we should preserve them for the national good. If we continue to allow this criminal waste of young Canadian lives as we have in the past, I say we are not worthy of the good earth which we inhabit; we are not worthy of the sunlight or the fresh air or the rich stores of food with which this land is blessed. Canada will never be great among the nations of the world if we continue to neglect to give the greatest consideration possible to the care of our children, our greatest national resource in times of peace.
To-day the armed forces are given all that it is possible for us to give. We give them adequate food, proper rest and sleep, good fresh air and exercise, medical treatment when needed, and mental training. That is only right, because these armed forces are defending the honour of Canada among the nations of the world; they are fighting to preserve the freedom not only of ourselves but of all mankind. That is in war. In peace should we not recognize that it is to our children we should transfer our greatest care?-for they are the army of peace.
I have tried to gather together the most recent figures available from- the Department of Pensions and National Health having to do with the care of women and children. Some of -these figures fall far short of the point where they give confidence to the nation that the best is being done at the present time, although some of us are apt to make allowances because of the war situation. Here is what I found.
In these days, to more than 279,000 families in Canada, in a single year the birth of a baby is the most important event of the year. Out of that number of families, in more than 22,570 the death of the mother or the loss of the baby brings tragedy. In 1942 there were 7,127 stillbirths, 14,637 infant deaths under one year, and 806 mothers who died. Each year more than 800 mothers die from causes connected with childbirth, .leaving more than 2,000 children motherless. Each year more than
7.000	babies are stillborn and more than 7,600 die in the first month of life. In addition an unknown number of women are injured in health, and children are handicapped in growth

and development, because of conditions associated with maternity.
In Canada about 20,000 confinements take place annually without the services of a doctor. In some provinces one birth out of every six is unattended by a physician. Out of every thousand births-these figures are still for the year 1942, the most recent I could get-25 children are stillborn and 54 more die in the first year of life, while 3 mothers are lost. In 1942, 2,842 Canadian babies died from premature birth. It is quite logical to assume that simple incubators would have done much to save the lives of many of those babies. We lost 2,048 babies from pneumonia, 380 from influenza, 1,249 from diarrhoea and enteritis, and 964 from congenital debility. The loss of life from whooping cough was 559; from diphtheria, 256; scarlet fever, 128 and measles, 130. The figure for measles covers children of all ages. There is no doubt that with proper care and the use of preventive measures a great proportion of this stupendous and unnecessary loss need not have occurred.
I would say that the group of officials in this new department charged with the special care of children should see to it, first, that just as we do for soldiers in the army we should provide for children, irrespective of the rank or position of their parents, those certain essentials which are necessary to build strong and healthy citizens.
First, and this is important, we should see to it that when men and women are about to become parents they should be examined to see if there are any hereditary diseases. This department should carry on work in all parts of Canada to see that mothers receive adequate food and rest and medical attention during the period of pregnancy and at the time of birth. These services should be the same for rural areas as for urban areas by the provision of travelling clinics.
Where mothers are working there should be edequate time allowed from employment without the loss of the job. There should be pay allowance for some weeks before and after the birth of the child. We want our birth rate to go up. We want children who are bom and raised on the soil of this country to grow up in the traditions which we cherish. We must not discourage working mothers from having children by penalizing them with the loss of their jobs. They should be permitted to carry on their work whatever it happens to be.
In a recent survey made in all plants in Canada where the united automobile workers' union is operating it was shown that 86 per cent of the women now working in war plants want to continue working after the war is

Department oj Health and Welfare
over, for one reason or another. Of the women who answered the questionnaire, 60 per cent were married, 45 per cent single and 5 per cent widows. Seventy-five per cent of all the wives of men in the armed services who answered this questionnaire wanted to continue at work. We must recognize the right of women to continue in the industrial field if they wish to do so. I see no reason why men should determine what women should do. Women should have the right as citizens to continue to work if they feel that they have reasons for doing so.
I believe that such a branch should set up and correlate with other sections of this department channels of social services whereby every child in Canada shall receive adequate supplies of milk, fruit and other food requirements as supplements wherever they are needed. That is not forcing anything upon anybody; it is merely giving them the opportunity to avail themselves of these things where they are necessary. This of course most usually would be done, I suppose, through pre-school creches and through the school lunch plan.
Again the branch could arrange for special clinics to deal with children's diseases, for we have seen that, contrary to popular belief, many infectious diseases of childhood are fatal. The education of mothers could be done through this branch, and certain aspects of child psychology and the care of special types of children could be dealt with adequately. Special open-air play and organized sports centres for little children could be organized; for quite often the little children do not have the opportunity for free play which they should have, because of the presence of older children on the playgrounds. All these and many other activities could rightly come within the purview of such a group of officials of this department or in correlation with other branches of this ministry.
We have had a slogan in war time: Everything for the fighting forces; everything for victory. Now that peace is coming I would like to have as the peace-time slogan of our nation, "Everything for our children and the coming generation." I am not overlooking for one moment the importance of the rehabilitation of our returned men and the responsibilities we have to them and to other sections of our society who may be in need of attention. But I do feel that the investment of public money is something which has to be most carefully considered. I ask the members of this house, as I did when I spoke previously: where is there any natural resource in Canada
in connection with which every investment made by the nation would bring as great a return as would come from proper care of the nation's children? Who can estimate the loss to Canada of those young lives so needlessly lost in the years that have gone by. What fine minds, what ability, what character as a nation we have lost in these young ones who might have made not only to Canada but to the whole world a contribution of inestimable value. Can we afford to run the chance of losing a Mendelssohn, a Madam Cure, an Einstein or a Canadian Shakespeare? How do we know that amongst those who were not born alive, or who died before reaching the age of one year, we did not lose some immortal Canadian who might have given, not only to us but to the whole world, of the riches of their minds? Because of our lack of concern for the health of mothers and the preservation of the life of mothers and their children, much has escaped us that can never be recaptured. Do not let us lose any more! Let us see to it that we have for them everything that is possible.
I wish the government had included a provision for such a thing as I suggest right within section 5 of this bill. If the government had drawn up such a section, it certainly would have received unanimous assent from all sides of the house. Often when amendments are introduced by an opposition member or even by some member on the government side of the house, they are automatically voted down because they are regarded as indication of a lack of confidence in the government. To-day I do not want to speak as an opposition member. I do not even want to speak as the representative in this house of North Battle-ford. I just want to speak as a woman. There are only two women members in this great chamber. The question that I have raised is one that is dear to the heart of women all over this country. I believe that there is not a woman anywhere but would agree that her heart was bound up in the welfare of the children of this nation. I speak not only for myself but for the women of Canada. I say also that I would try to speak on behalf of those many little mouths which have been stopped by death through carelessness and lack of care in Canada, and which, had they the power to speak, might have spoken more eloquently than I ever could on this and many other matters of vital importance, and might have given the leadership to us that we so badly need.
I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a political question. It is not even a question of asking for a further expenditure of money. Therefore, sir, with your permission
4868	COMMONS
Department of Health and Welfare
I wish to introduce an amendment, moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Cartier, as follows:
That section 5 be amended by adding the following as paragraph (j):
(j) the setting up of a branch of child welfare to deal specifically with all matters relating to the health and general welfare of children, some administrative officials of which branch shall be women.
I hope this amendment will have support from all sides of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the amendment I think I should speak on it first and then deal with the matter raised by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.
May I say at once that I appreciate the contribution made by the hon. member for North Battleford to the discussion of the prenatal, natal and post-natal care of Canadian children. But if the hon. member will look at section 5 of the bill she will find in the first two or three lines that the duties, powers and functions of the minister "shall extend to and include all matters relating to the promotion or preservation of the health, social security and social welfare of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction." My hon. friend will realize that there are many matters in relation to child welfare over which the parliament of Canada and the government of Canada have no jurisdiction.
One would infer from some of the remarks of my hon. friend, beautifully expressed as they were, and very sympathetically-and I agree with their general tenor-that there was no provision at the present time in the department of health in regard to child welfare. There is a separate division of child and maternal hygiene, and that division will be continued. It is one of the ablest divisions to-day in the department of health. My hon. friend will find at page 48 of the report on the work of the Department of Pensions and National Health a comprehensive description of the functions and duties and scope and responsibilities of that branch of the department. No finer official work has been accomplished in the health field of Canada in the last twenty years than the work of Doctor Couture, who is at the head of the department His publication entitled "The Canadian Mother and Child" is famous all over Canada. We have issued a hundred thousand copies of that publication in English and in French. Every day of my life I receive from humble homes throughout Canada applications for that publication, and letters of thanks when it has been received.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: Everyone in the chamber will endorse that statement, I believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am grateful to my hon. friend for his remark. I want to remove this afternoon a twofold possibility of misapprehension. One is that the department of health is not paying attention to this important phase of child welfare, as far as child welfare comes within the competence of this parliament or of this government. Our hearts are all with the ideals expressed by the hon. member for North Battleford. Every hon. member wants conditions improved. I have been looking at the comparative figures relating to Australia and New Zealand, and we in Canada compare with them very well. We are far ahead of some other countries in regard to infant mortality and live births, and so long as we have men like Doctor Couture in charge, so long as we have a sympathetic government, and a kind-hearted parliament, as we have here, I have no doubt that Canada will go ahead from year to year in this most important field.
While I am on my feet I wish to say a word or two with regard to the very moving appeal of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. He made one last year which had a deep impression upon me.

It has been repeated over and over again from different sides of the house, that we should not in this federal parliament seek to invade the jurisdiction of the provinces; and it is well known that many, if not, indeed, all of the provinces regard child welfare as coming specifically within their jurisdiction.
I do not wish to raise any question of jurisdiction, but what I would say is this. The creation of this department of national health and welfare, contemplating as it does very close association with the provinces, will help to remove many difficulties which now arise out of jurisdiction. On these questions of child welfare, it is to be expected that what, in the end, will best serve the interests of the provinces and the dominion, alike, will be furthered by having a federal department which can keep in touch generally with all of these matters, and the duty of which will be to help coordinate them with the provinces,
and in that way avoid overlapping as well as ensure that there will be no omissions of essential services.

I would say first to the Minister of Pensions and National Health that I had no intention whatever of leaving the inference that I was not aware of such provisions as are already being made with regard to child welfare under the department which now exists. The last time I spoke on this matter I mentioned the book for mothers and children and recommended it very highly. But I feel that unless we definitely and specifically state that a certain group of officials within this department shall have the sole assignment of these matters relating to child welfare, it may be that in the general scheme we shall not have just what I would envisage. On the other hand I do not wish to have any group of officials in this department overriding the rights of the provinces; that of course would be wrong. But we find a great deal of inequality among the provinces, and I would hope that such a group of officials in this department could do something to equalize the chances for mothers and children in the various provinces.
I will quote a few figures to prove that inequalities exist. In 1942 the number of infant deaths per thousand live births, by provinces, was:
British Columbia	 35
Alberta	 38
Ontario	 40
Saskatchewan	 43
Prince Edward Island	 50
Manitoba	 51
Nova Seo-tia	 58
Quebec	 70
Newr Brunswick	 77
In some of the smaller and poorer provinces the opportunity or the likelihood of a child getting good care is not as great as in other provinces; and I believe that some correlation on the part of officials could do something to eliminate that condition.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health has said that so far as our infant mortality rate is concerned we do not stand badly in comparison with other countries. Let me again quote figures to show how we do stand in that regard. In 1942 the number of deaths per thousand live births was 54, which is a record for Canada. I will say this, that ever since 1926 the mortality rate has progressively decreased, yet the number of

Department of Health and Welfare
deaths per thousand live births was 54, as compared with these figures in other countries: United States 40'4; New Zealand 28-7; England and Wales, 49. So that the Canadian death rate is considerably higher than that of these other countries. We still have need to continue and to do more than we are doing for the preservation of the lives of our children.
I did not envisage by this amendment the expenditure of any further moneys. The purpose of the amendment is merely that within the provision made for this department of health we should have certain officials whose efforts should be directed specifically to questions of maternal and child welfare, that they should carry on under the department, using only such sums out of the general funds of the department as might be allocated to them. They should be specifically given that work and their job should be to correlate their efforts with those of the provincial health department in an endeavour to bring about a general betterment of conditions and to establish greater equality of opportunity in the preservation of life in the various provinces.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I would like to go back to the subject which was introduced at the beginning of the debate by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, supported by the hon. member for St. Boniface. Perhaps this hour will go down in history as one of the most momentous in the life, not of this session only but of this parliament, altogether transcending in importance even the question of the war. For while the war is a terrible disaster, involving a terrible loss of life, it does not go on for ever, whereas this dread disease will continue for ever unless a cure is found for it, and it will take an ever-increasing toll. I think the house owes a great debt to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the hon. member for St. Boniface for having introduced the subject. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie spoke with the intensity of a man who was himself a victim; yet I realize just what it cost the hon. member for St. Boniface to take a stand opposite to that of many of his colleagues in the house.
I think it cannot be denied that this man Davidson has, what they call in the vernacular, got something. Take these two hon. members of parliament. I have known them for many years. They have established a reputation for their probity and intelligence. Are we to suggest that they are crooks or humbugs, that they do not know what they are talking about? One of them is a medical man who has enjoyed a long career, and the record of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, who went to, I suppose, the highest authorities in the world, the Mayo Brothers, is well known. It is common usage for some doctors to say that when So-and-so says he was cured by this treatment or that, he did not have cancer; it was just a mistake in diagnosis, he only thought that he had it, or something of the kind. But when men and women, as recorded by the hon. member on a previous occasion, have gone to and been certified by men like the Mayo Brothers to be definitely suffering from incurable and inoperable cancer, then surely we must agree that the resulting recovery was due to something more than idle chance.
Doctor Davidson has spent a long time in that city and is well known. He built up a practice for himself and engaged in the ordinary practice of healing people. He spent his own time and money in developing what perhaps came to him originally by chance in the line of cancer research. Are we to suggest that this man is a crook? If so, then he ought to be exposed. If his methods are good and his statements are true, or even if there is the shadow of a possibility of his being able to

Department of Health and Welfare
produce a remedy, certainly he ought to be surrounded with every comfort and men to learn at his feet. Far better to do that than keep him curing children of mumps in order to make a living.
Why say that we cannot afford to spend a little of the taxpayers' money on this? Look back into history. I do not want to attack the medical men. That would be very foolish when I am trying to get their support in this matter. It is a notorious fact-I do not know why it is so-that history tells us medical men are, in the dictionary sense, not in the political sense, extremely conservative. It has to be demonstrated beyond the shadow of a doubt, not in hundreds of cases but in thousands of cases, before they will admit the possibility of any startling discovery. That was true of the man who discovered anaesthetics, and the man who discovered the use of vaccine in smallpox, and later on, Pasteur. They were not exactly prosecuted, but they were sneered at. It was said that they were cranks, and it was impossible that it should be so. I read just the other day a story to the effect that in Boston a number of years ago they proposed to prosecute a man because he had been advocating the selling of shares in a ridiculous company which proposed to operate what is now known as the telephone. An editorial in one of the papers said how ridiculous it was to think of such a device, that such a device could not possibly succeed; and even if sound could be sent over a wire, of what practical use would it be? There is a man who was not crucified, but he was prosecuted because he had a little greater vision than perhaps other people.
Davidson was sent a questionnaire, a real official questionnaire, the same as you get when you apply for a passport. They want to know what your wife's father-in-law mother's name was, and so on, bearing strictly upon whether you can get a passport to go to the United States or not. When you have it all filled out and get it certified by a notary public they write to the notary public and say: "Jones said that you signed that paper. Are you a notary public, and did you sign it?" That happened to me. Doctor Davidson got the questionnaire and I suppose-I did not see it but I got the gist of it-they went thoroughly into the situation. Perhaps they asked him: "When did you first begin the investigation of this particular case, or of that particular case? Was it on a Tuesday or a Monday?" The doctor, being a busy man and having to make his own living, and being near the end of his life, replied possibly more curtly than he need to have done. To some particular questions he answered: "I did not keep the 
data. I did not presume twenty years ago or ten years ago that I would be subjected to this investigation, and I did not keep the data; but I do know that such-and-such results have ensued." The answer then was, "We do not feel we are justified in recommending that public money be spent." That was the recommendation, and yet we are squandering it by the millions every hour in the prosecution of destruction.
This afternoon someone passed a remark- I did not get the exact wording of it-at the expense of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. The committee smiled-smiled in this day and generation at this tragedy. There should be no doubt as to whether we need to investigate this thing. If Doctor Davidson has anything at all, let us pursue it to the utmost. This man is going to die. He is an old man, and he is going to carry his knowl-** edge and information to the grave with him. Then we shall look at each other and wonder why. Somebody will blame somebody else, and ask, why did we not do something? I know it will be said: What have I to do with it? What do I know about it? He is only an ignorant layman anyway. I am not dealing with medical matters as a medical man. I am dealing with them as a layman. If we do not continue this discussion, someone else will get up, as did the hon. member for North Battleford, and introduce another subject, and that will be the end of the presentation made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie; but if we talk long enough the government will say, of course, that a private member cannot introduce any proposal looking to the expenditure of public money. If that is to be the case, the opportunity will be gone and we never know when it may be recovered.
Parliament is going to adjourn shortly, and perhaps a parliament of new .men will come back. Some of the present hon. members may not be here. In the meantime this man will die. It is said that God helps those who help themselves. I have a suggestion to offer to this committee. If the government in their narrow-minded fashion will not hold this investigation, how about our doing it? There are 245 members here. If we each put up $50 that would be enough to keep the thing running for a year. Some of us could not afford to put up the $50, but others could easily put up more. I suggest that we take it on ourselves. I should , be glad to put up $50 in cooperation with other hon. members in order to help this thing out in the meantime. We will not stand on the order of our going but we will start something, and we will do it.
I am sure the press would endorse' it. If the

Department oj Health and Welfare
members of the government saw that we were willing to attempt it, perhaps they would take an interest in it and investigate it.
This is something much bigger than just a petty amendment to a bill. It is a question that means the lives of millions of people in the future. To what better use could we and the government put our money than that of having this matter investigated? If this man is found to be a crook, I will not begrudge the money; it will be well spent in finding out the facts. I am not suggesting that he is a crook. The people who made the recommendation against him did not suggest anything of the kind; they simply say he is not proceeding along the old standard lines. They say he did not answer the questions in the exact way they were drawn up, and therefore they do not recommend the spending of public money. I suggest that we have the courage of our convictions, and if the government will not do anything, let us do it ourselves. It would be a fine gesture, and we should be giving a lead to the house and the country in doing something which would be more justified than a lot of the measures we have been debating this session.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I desire to make reference to paragraph (e) of section 5. In order that there may be greater clarity I think I ought to read the section as it now stands in the bill. Section 5 reads:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister shall extend to and include all matters relating to the promotion or preservation of the health, social security and social welfare of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters:
(e) the supervision of federal public buildings and offices with a view to conserving and promoting the health of the civ-il4 servants and other government employees therein.
If the subject matter dealt with in paragraph (e) had not been set out particularly, the point I desire to make would have been covered adequately by the general provisions of the early part of the section, but since it has been particularly mentioned I feel that I should make some reference to it. This is a very narrow way of expressing the problem that we hope will be dealt with. It would seem to limit the minister's jurisdiction to the actual buildings in which public employees work and would appear to exclude such matters as recreation, nutrition and so on. I am sure most of us hope that the matter of the recreation of our citizens will be taken up much more extensively in the post-war era than has been the case heretofore. Already the em-nlovees of the dominion government in
Ottawa have a recreational association of their own which is doing splendid work in this respect. The programme envisaged and undertaken by this association promises to be most helpful, and I think has been advanced sufficiently to indicate its beneficial nature Certainly it is an important part of the social welfare of the people of Canada. It is my hope that, as we go on, the government, and particularly this new department and its minister, will take active steps to advance that work with respect to government employees. I do not desire to elaborate on that subject at the moment, but I wish to emphasize its importance.	[DOT]
There are other, similar subjects to be dealt with, such as nutrition. In future years I hope the government will extend its activities in those fields of public health and nutrition. Nevertheless the clause as it now stands H expresses the authority of the minister in very narrow terms. If there is no legal objection- and I see none according to the rules of the house-and no objection on the part of the government I would suggest that the words "the supervision of federal public buildings and offices with a view to conserving and promoting" be struck out and these words substituted: "the conservation and promotion of", and that the word "therein" at the end of the subsection be deleted. It would then read: "the conservation and promotion of the health of the civil servants and other government employees." I think that would more adequately describe what is intended to be covered by this subsection and we would be left in the position that it could not be argued at some future time that the jurisdiction of the minister was limited to the narrow question of the supervision of public buildings.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend no doubt has observed, the clause to which he has just referred is in the existing act as subsection (e) of part 2. I am quite agreeable to asking my colleague the Minister of Pensions and National Health to move as an amendment what my hon. friend has suggested; to substitute for the words "the supervision of federal public buildings and offices with a view to conserving and promoting" the words, "the conservation and promotion of" and to strike out the word "therein" at the end of the subsection. Then

Department oj Health and Welfare
subsection (e) would read: "the conservation and promotion of the health of the civil servants and other government employees."

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: I move accordingly.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext: I do not wi^h to oppose this amendment, but at present the section covers "the supervision of federal public buildings and offices" for certain purposes. Perhaps this is not the correct place to bring up this matter, but I must say I was surprised the other day, when I went into the east block, to discover that it had no adequate modern fire prevention appliances, particularly no sprinkler system. It seems to me that if we are going to supervise or promote the health of civil servants we should also look after their lives. It may be said that this is properly a matter for the Department of Public Works, but I suggest to the minister that he consider the advisability of installing a sprinkler system in each block, because in my opinion conditions are not satisfactory as far as fire hazards are concerned.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would not want to oppose the extension of power suggested in the amendment, but it seems to me that the amendment lacks something in reference to the supervision of public buildings by the ministry of health. In my humble opinion this government has no cause to be proud of the situation in regard to ventilation, fire protection and general health conditions in the public buildings of the city of Ottawa.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext: Even in this chamber.

maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Such buildings as the Langevin block, the east block and many of the temporary buildings, with their poor ventilation, would not do credit to any employer, let alone the dominion government. As a matter of fact, conditions even in this house, during these warm days, do not contribute to the comfort, well-being or even the mental equilibrium of hon. members. I believe the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa West is exceptionally good, but it Should include some part of the original subsection, to cover the supervision of public buildings in regard to matters of public health. Right now, with this hot weather, we hear many complaints in regard to ventilation from civil servants who are working under conditions of congestion. I have had some particular eases brought to my attention, one of which I might mention. An employee of the government entered the service in 1938 with a first-class health certificate, but when he attempted to join the army in 1942 he was discovered to have a lung condition which was diagnosed as

tuberculosis. He went to the hospital in Ottawa, where I believe he still is, where it was discovered that he had contracted his tuberculosis by contact while in the government employ. After a considerable time he was able to get a pension. On investigating the case I found that the conditions under which he was working were, to say the least, such as would make the contraction of tuberculosis quite possible. In other words, the ventilation was quite bad.
We hear complaints nearly every day from civil servants working in the temporary buildings, particularly those along the north side of Wellington street. For security reasons it is necessary that the windows be locked at night, and when the staff come to work in the morning they find their rooms have been closed without being properly ventilated. The result is that the rooms are overheated. This new department should have the special responsibility of supervising the working conditions of government employees. The government should be a model employer, and should provide healthy working conditions rather than the haphazard system we have at the present time.
I suggest, that the amendment is a good one, but it should carry with it some special direction as to the supervision of public buildings and offices for health purposes.

I want to support what the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the hon. member for St. Boniface have said regarding Doctor Davidson. speechtext:
I was starting to say a few minutes ago, when we were dealing with the amendment which has just been passed, that I believe clause 5 of the bill should have had something new written into it so far as powers are concerned. As the bill stands, while the idea of shuffling the departments around and bringing related matters under one

ministry is a good one, really that is all we are doing in this bill, namely, providing an administrative reshuffling. Already during the debate, to-day a number of new services have been proposed, and one amendment has been ruled out of order, but they suggest some of the powers and functions and duties which I think should have been provided for under clause 5. May I name some that I have jotted down?
First of all there is the subject which my colleague the hon. member for Selkirk has just mentioned, preventive medicine; second, powers in connection with the training of medical personnel; third, powers to coordinate our medical services and see to it that they are properly distributed throughout the country according to the needs of our people, particularly those in the outlying areas. Then, too, I think there should be included in this clause powers with respect to the building of additional hospital facilities. I believe also powers with respect to the subjects mentioned by the hon. member for North Battleford should be included here in more positive terms, namely, powers to deal with child and maternity care.
I would add that in this day and generation it seems to me that some real initiative should be taken in the matter of nutrition. We have heard a good deal said to-day about the possibilities of the nutritional treatment of cancer. It is also well known that there are tremendous possibilities of improving the general health of the whole community by research in the field of nutrition with a view to improving the diet of our people. We know as a matter of fact that under the most trying circumstances during the period of intense attacks upon Great Britain the health of her people has been maintained, and this enabled them to stand the strain of the war, largely because of the work which the British government has done in the field of nutrition. It seems to me that in the post-war period we ought in the name of health to be taking the initiative in this field.
My whole point is that if this bill is to be more than just an administrative reshuffling, we should have something new added along the lines that I have proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE

If my hon. friend will examine the introductory part of clause 5 and then examine paragraph (a) he will find that every single thing he mentioned is already covered by the bill. The training of medical personnel is not altogether within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, as my

The coordination of medical services and their distribution is definitely a provincial responsibility, but is being carried out in war time through the federal government by means of the medical assignment board. Ordinarily it must be done in time of peace in cooperation with the provincial authorities.
The provision of additional hospital facilities relates itself, of course, to any national scheme of health insurance.
Child and maternal care is amply taken care of now in the department.
In regard to nutrition, there is a special branch of the department, nutritional services, which has been carrying on excellent work, particularly in the last year or two, throughout the dominion. It has received the commendation of every single province.
Every one of the services mentioned by my hon. friend that comes within the jurisdiction of the federal authorities and of this new department is provided for in clause 5 as now drafted.

speechtext: For this reason among others, that it is far better draftsmanship and far more comprehensive to set out the purposes in general words rather than in specific words because, when you start to enumerate things, you are almost bound to leave out something or else set out a class of things which will be found to be. inadequate with the progress of medical science and with the development of cooperation between the dominion and the provinces. maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am afraid that I have to agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I had thought that this bill was going to mean something new, but as I see it now it is merely transferring everything of a civilian nature in the Department of Pensions and National Health to this department and assigning veterans' affairs exclusively to another department. I agree absolutely with the purpose for which the department is being formed, but we are not going to make much progress if all that is involved is a reallocation of functions between different departments.
The parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister is right to a certain extent in saying that it is sometimes dangerous to try to be too specific in legislation, but on the other hand if all our legislation were couched in
general terms you could not pin anyone down to anything and as a result you would get nothing done. It is a very odd way of shifting responsibility. In this field of social security generally we are setting up a lot of departments, and unless we are specific about some things there will be a tendency on the part of one department to shift to another things which should be their own responsibility. I thought the hon. member for North Battle-ford made a very strong case this afternoon for the setting up of a branch in this department and holding it absolutely responsible for the better care of our children in all its phases. This is a matter about which we should be specific. While we have a department-we realize that-and this new machinery is taking over its functions, let it not be forgotten that the minister's department has been in existence for the last twenty years, and the figures cited by the hon. member would lead anyone to believe that the job which has been done is far from satisfactory.
In the next place, I believe that we have fallen down in the field of research in preventive medicine. Although the minister's department has included for some considerable time a branch of research into industrial diseases and so forth, its operations are largely confined to the laboratory. Its work has not got through to the people. As I visualize the new department, unless the discoveries which have been made in the laboratories are made available to the people we shall have accomplished nothing more than a mere reshuffling of machinery.
The matter raised by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie a year ago in this house, and again this afternoon, is of great concern all over the world. I thought he made a very strong case. He is a living example of the absolute necessity for an investigation, and I say, an investigation by the dominion government. We are merely shelving our responsibility by throwing it into the lap of the medical profession. The medical profession have something to sell, and so long as the rules of the game are as they are, it is their prerogative to sell it; but it is the responsibility of the government, particularly the health department, to make available to the people anything which will alleviate misery and distress. That is their function. If Doctor Davidson of Winnipeg has something of value to the people of Canada, it is the responsibility of the health department to investigate that without any reference to medical societies throughout Canada. There are competent medical men within the department who should examine it and report direct to the minister.

It is known as A.C.S., and according to the reports we have received it is working miracles in Russia. I understand that there is some available in the United States for experimental purposes. I wrote the minister the other day about it. I am not going to press the question, but I am doing what I can to find out about the availability of supply.
There is no use in developing medical science unless its discoveries are made available to the people. The purpose is to relieve misery and suffering. If we are going to develop a lot of things to relieve pain and then lock

them up in a laboratory somewhere or sell them at a price which is beyond the means of the average individual, we shall not have accomplished much.
Further, to segregate problems of a general nature from those which relate to the veterans of the last war and this war, without the intention of expanding under the new department our work in the field of national health, will not be of much value. If the minister is handicapped by certain limitations from pushing his work for the health of the Canadian people as it should be pushed, he should let us know, make appropriate proposals in this house, and have the house grant him the necessary authority before the present session closes. As the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has pointed out, a number of hon. members who are here to-day and have discussed these matters for the past four, years will not sit in the next parliament, and it will take the new house perhaps four years to understand exactly what the problems are. Now is the time to do these things. I do not believe anyone in this house is in disagreement with any other member on matters of public health. Everyone is prepared to support the government to any extent they want to go with respect to making medical science available to the people of Canada,

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subtopic: CREATION OF DEPARTMENT FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF SOCIAL SECURITY AND WELFARE

As regards the question which came up last year and wTas again raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, concerning Doctor Davidson, the inference has been left by certain speakers to-day that the Department of Pensions and National Health took no action with reference to his request. Department oj Health and Welfare
medical committee of the national research council. The chairman of that committee is one of the best-known surgeons and medical men in Canada-Doctor Best, who was associated with Doctor Banting in the discovery of insulin; and members of that committee-
I am not speaking as a medical man; I am only a layman-are some of the most brilliant scientists in Canada to-day. Before his death Sir Frederick Banting went thoroughly into this whole question and, I believe, discussed it with Doctor Davidson personally. An hon. MEMBER; Will the minister tell me whether this treatment has been tried out by any person other than Doctor Davidson?

The question came up again; I endeavoured to obtain an investigation in the province of Manitoba, through the university of Manitoba, and they were approached by the department. I took the matter up and was told by the Department of Justice that we had no authority to investigate such questions since they were entirely within the provincial sphere. I have the written documents in my files to that effect. When, therefore, it is said that nothing has been done by the Department of Pensions and National Health, I assert that I did everything that was within our constitutional power. Take the province of Ontario. For years they have been carrying on cancer research, and any province in Canada can
properly, within the ambit of the constitution, cany on cancer research; but the dominion authority cannot, except by cooperation or invitation, step into the provincial field either in the matter of cancer or in the matter of any other malady, and carry out an investigation on its own.

There is one way, however, by which the matter can be dealt with without any of the difficulties which the minister mentions with respect to the constitution. There is Deer Lodge hospital, Winnipeg; there is Christie Street hospital, Toronto, and there are many other military hospitals in the country. Cancer is not confined to civilians.
It is a disease that has afflicted many of those who have been discharged from or are at present connected with the armed forces. If * my understanding is correct, one of the things which those who support Doctor Davidson's treatment desire is that he shall be given an opportunity, in some hospital ward, to have

Department oj Health and Welfare
his experiments carried out in a practical manner. I suggest to the minister, so far as constitutionality is concerned, that he would have the power as Minister of Pensions and National Health to have this done in any of the military hospitals in Canada. I do not know whether this is practical, and I have hesitated all along to pose as in any degree an expert in this matter, because I know there are none of us laymen who are experts. I have heard some laymen in debates like this speak as though they were experts, but for myself, I do not pose as one. At the same time, I should like to make sure that nothing is being overlooked because of the point of view of the constitution, for I do not think red tape should be allowed to stand in the *way of further experimentation toward the end of helping humanity.

speechtext: My name having been mentioned, I should like to make a few remarks with reference to what the leader of the opposition has just said about Deer Lodge hospital. This man, through injuries received in the last war, developed cancer, and he is now getting treatment for it in that hospital.
