maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Article I covers it. It reads:
The taxes referred to in this convention are:
(a)	for the United States of America: the federal estate taxes;
(b)	for Canada: the taxes imposed under the Dominion Succession Duty Act.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
We are not talking about taxes; we are talking about the effect of the overriding provisions of this convention. We are not talking about taxes in section 3; we are talking about the effect in law of the convention. I had intended to refer to that before the hon. member for Essex East rose. I suggest that the words "and the operation of any other law" are too wide. You cannot legislate here to override laws relating to the situs of property passed by a province. I lay down that general proposition
Mr.,GIBSON: I quite agree with that, but for the purpose of the Dominion Succession Duty Act we can lay down what property is to be taxed. That is all we are doing.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: In so far as the tax is concerned, but here you are passing a general statute. Have the law officers of the crown considered this section?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: This has been submitted to the Department of Justice and has been approved by them.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I have no doubt that is true, but has this particular feature been called to their attention? Have they reviewed it fully? After the statement, "in the event of any inconsistency between the provisions of this act or of the said convention and the operation of any other law", the section goes on to state, "and in particular the law relating to the taxation of the succession to property". That should be limited to the taxation by the dominion of the succession to property. You cannot pass a law here that relates to the taxation, by the province, of the succession to property, and that is what is being attempted here. The provisions of this section are too wide.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Section 3 is not attempting to override provincial legislation.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: That is the effect of the general language.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: The section states that if this convention is inconsistent with any other law, and if we assume that that includes provincial legislation, then the provisions of this bill and the convention shall to the extent of the inconsistency not prevail.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Shall
prevail.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I have not heard the whole discussion, but I am wondering if the hon. member for York-Sunbury and1 the minister would feel that the problem they are considering now would be solved by adding after the words " any other law," the clause that we found in section 5 of bill No. 149, which was considered this afternoon and which reads, " over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction."

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I agree.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Would that not solve it?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
I think it would. I am pointing out that this legislature cannot deal 100 per cent with the whole question when it must limit itself to its own jurisdiction.
Tax Convention Act

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: If inconsistencies in the Ontario succession duty act cropped up they might pass something that did not conform with this convention.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: This does not deal with the Ontario succession duty act.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It says, " any other law."

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It deals with the succession to property.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: The phrase I had in mind was, " over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction." If it is needless we should not put it in, but I believe it would clarify beyond question the point that has been raised.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I urge the minister to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Parry Sound.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Property and civil rights is a matter for the jurisdiction of the provinces, and if we put that in they might say that that is a matter over which the dominion parliament has no jurisdiction.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: You have taken jurisdiction under section 91 over the succession to property in your succession duty act. You have the widest possible powers of taxation. I am not raising this point just for fun or for'the purposes of obstruction; I do so because I really think there is objection to the form of the section as drafted. In the light of the discussion I think the minister would be well advised if he reviewed the situation. I am not going to labour the point any farther. I believe we have made our position quite clear. If you try to override provincial statutes you will run foul of Mr. Duplessis and a lot of other people.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Whatever we would be overriding would be only for the purposes of avoiding double taxation between Canada and the United States, not to change the general law of this country.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: The object might be excellent, but the language is not appropriate. I think the suggestion offered by Ihe hon. member for Parry Sound is a sound one. That phrase is included in the health act, and I think we should limit our attempts at taking jurisdiction to the constitutional powers of the dominion.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
There is now pending in Ontario some important legislation in connection with the Ontario succession duty act as to the right of taxation of mining shares where a resident of New York dies owning mining shares in an Ontario company and

there are transfer offices of the company in Toronto and in New York. Important questions are pending now as to the right of the province to levy a tax upon shares where the deceased died in the United States and was a resident of that country.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
This is a
vexed problem.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It is in my view.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I would not want to limit this in that way because it might limit us more than is desirable.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I think I would take advice on it.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I cannot agree.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
You cannot hoist yourself by your own boot-straps and you cannot seize jurisdiction just by putting it in an act of parliament; you must have inherent jurisdiction under the constitution. I would play safe and limit it to the constitutional powers of the federal authorities, but I am not going to argue the matter any farther. I think you will run into trouble if you do not do as has been suggested.
There is just one other point I want to refer to under section 4 and then I shall be through. What are the orders and regulations which the minister has in mind and which are, in his opinion, necessary for the purpose of carrying out the convention? Powers to make orders and regulations should not be so general as this. They should be limited in scope and extent. But this is wide open, within, of course, the terms of the convention. I should like to know what orders or regulations the minister has in mind which, in his opinion, may be necessary for the purpose of carrying out the convention.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: That really refers to the administrative work of carrying out the convention, the preparation of forms, for instance, and providing for whatever other action is necessary to carry out the convention's terms.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Then why not say, "necessary for the due administration of the convention"? That has a narrowing effect. Under this section the minister has very wide powers to make any kind of regulation he likes so long as it is made in carrying out the convention. If it is meant to be purely administrative, why not say so?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
It is really the same type of form that we have in the bill respecting the income tax convention. It is more or less a routine section.

Tax Convention Act

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I took the same objection then. It is no answer to say that because we did it in a previous statute we are going to do it in this. On principle that is no answer at all. Because you have done it over a period of thirty or forty years even does not constitute an answer. Bad legislation should not be placed on the statute books at all, and I think this is bad draftsmanship. The powers to make rules and regulations should be limited strictly to the purposes of the administration of the act. Some minister may come along and say: I have power under section 4 to make a regulation that goes beyond administration.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Only "for the purpose of carrying out the said convention."

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I realize that it must be with this subject-matter in view. That is all that that means. I deprecate the practice that is becoming more and more prevalent in departmental legislation of giving these extraordinary powers to ministers to legislate, because that is what it is. I shall never cease, so long as I am a member of this house, to raise my voice against this delegation of power except for purely administrative purposes, and the language of the section is not within the ambit of that statement.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I cannot share the view of the hon. member in that respect. Let me put it in this way. The minister who makes any regulation under the authority of section 4 must confine himself to the necessities of carrying out the convention which we are about to approve as law. The minute he made a regulation which stepped outside of the purpose "of carrying out the said convention", he would be travelling outside section 4.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: He may make such regulations as are in his opinion necessary. It is only his opinion.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: In all these matters where a minister is given power to make regulations to carry out a statute-and I suppose we have a dozen like this-it is always a matter of opinion by the minister, advised by his advisers, as to whether a particular regulation that he thinks ought to be put into effect is one which comes within his authority given to him by statute. So that I would not be alarmed because it is a matter of opinion.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: But he is the sole judge.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: But the courts will set him straight if he makes a regulation that he has not the right to make. You run that risk, I say with all respect to my hon. friend, whenever you authorize the making of regulations by order in council to provide the machinery for carrying out a particular piece of legislation.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I think I am in agreement with a certain part of what the hon. member for Parry Sound has said, but he will agree with me that this is a delegated authority and that the powers are wide open within a certain ambit. Should they not be restricted? That is the only point I am raising.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: What sort of language would the hon. member restrict it to?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I would restrict it by express words, "necessary to the administration of the convention". But I am not going to do the drafting.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: We are restricted by the wording to carrying out the terms of the convention.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I do not think so. It says, "in his opinion, necessary for the purpose of carrying out the said convention." They may find that the convention lacks something which they want done, something outside the ambit of the convention.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: We could well drop out the words "in his opinion", and make it definite.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: There is another question I should like to ask. Who is going to attack any of these regulations? That is a poser. The subject is not going to attack them unless they are clearly without. jurisdiction. Once you give power to an executive to legislate, and that is what we are doing here-

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Somebody must have
authority to make regulations to administer these laws.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Not necessarily. I can remember that when the discussion over the mobilization regulations was taking place in the house I pointed out that the government was taking power to legislate under a general authority, whereas on a previous occasion the regulations were brought down and submitted to parliament. That is the way it ought to be done. We are too prone in this country to-day, as they have been in days gone by in England, to delegate authority to legislate to the executive. It is the principle I am contending for. I know that in war time there must be a relaxation of the rule to a degree, but there certainly is a principle involved. I am not going to labour the point. I suppose that this will go through if I were to stay here until to-morrow morning, and I do not propose to do that on a hot night. I have pointed out what I consider to be a weakness in the section as drafted. I think the principle is bad and



Tax Convention Act
the minister would be well advised if he restricted his powers to pure matters of administration of the subject matter of the convention.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: These regulations do not have to be printed in the Canada Gazette or tabled. In similar statutes I have noticed that provision is made that the regulations must be printed in the Canada Gazette and also be laid on the table within a certain number of days after parliament meets. But these regulations will just be hidden away. Nobody will know what they are until they spring at the people right out of the blue.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Unless
publicity is given to them how is a lawyer to know what the law is?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I quite agree that there must be some publication.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I think the point is well taken.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
If I may read from the bill we had before us this afternoon, bill No. 149, an act to establish a Department of National Health and Welfare, section 10 reads:
Regulations made under this act shall forthwith after approval by the governor in council be published in the Canada Gazette and laid before parliament within fifteen days after they are made if parliament is then sitting, and, if not, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
I should like to read section 58, subsection 2, of the Dominion Succession Duty Act:
(2) The minister may make any regulations deemed necessary for carrying this act into effect, and in particular may make regulations:
(a)	prescribing forms and providing for the use thereof;
(b)	prescribing the amount, form and manner in which security shall be furnished;
(c)	prescribing what rule, method and standard of mortality and of value, and what rate of interest shall be used in determining the value of annuities, terms of years, life estates, income, and interests in expectancy; and
(d)	authorizing the commissioner to exercise such of the powers conferred by this act, as may, in the opinion of the minister, be conveniently exercised by the commissioner.
These regulations are provided for in the succession duty act and they are published in the Gazette.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: By authority of statute?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Not by the authority of
statute, but the succession duty branch does do that.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: By custom?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: By custom.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
But there is no provision in this bill before us?
Mr. GIBSON; No. There is no provision for it in the Succession Duty Act either, but it is the custom to do that.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); The minister will observe that while the Succession Duty Act provides in the opening paragraph for general powers of order and regulation, yet the effect of the whole section read together is to limit the powers of the minister to the particular subject-matters enumerated, and I think he would find that the court would hold him to that. At least that would be my interpretation of the section. I think the minister ought at least to publish these orders and regulations.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that we do that as a matter of course; we publish them in the Canada Gazette.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
I do not think we should
depend on "matter of course." There should be a provision in the bill itself so that we shall know that it will be done. I move:
That another section be added to this bill to read as follows:
"Orders and regulations made under this act by the Minister of National Revenue shall be published in the Canada Gazette and laid before parliament within fifteen days after they are made, if parliament is then sitting, and if not. within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof."

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Would it not be well to
put in the word "forthwith"?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I intended to put that in.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
That could be added to
section 4 without creating a new section.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Oh, yes,
that is a matter of form.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: I have no objection to adding that to section 4.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Will the amendment be put in writing?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: The hon. member has not had time to put it in writing. We will do so if you demand it. Will the minister go back and give the same consideration to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Parry Sound, to put in the words, "within the jurisdiction of this parliament," where he suggested it?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
No. I do not think I
would be willing to do that.

Tax Convention Act

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Has this convention been
approved and declared to have the force of law by the government of the United States?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: No, it has not been approved yet. It has been signed of coarse. But it is before congress.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Does the minister know the
approximate date when it will be approved?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
I understand that congress
has been adjourned until the 1st of August.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: If congress does not approve it, what then? Is there a provision in the convention for approval?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Article XIV states:
1. This convention shall be ratified and the instruments of ratification shall be exchanged at Washington as soon as possible.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: Should wre not add a clause to this bill that it will be brought into effect when it is promulgated by order in council?

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: After ratification by the United States.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Suppose congress never
approves it.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
I do not
believe that the proper consideration has been given to this whole matter. This may never be ratified by the United States; yet it is the law of Canada. Somebody has slipped.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
It comes into effect after
it has been ratified by both countries.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It is deemed to have come into effect in 1941.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It says it shall be ratified and the instruments of ratification shall be exchanged as soon as possible. The convention shall be deemed to have come into effect on June 14, 1941; and the minute this bill passes the Canadian parliament it is binding on Canada, and it is not binding on the United States until it is ratified by the United States Senate. It is in the form of a treaty. It looks to me like very loose workmanship.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
Article XIV covers it. It
does not become operative between the two countries until it has been ratified by the legislative bodies of both countries.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: It does not say that.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext:
No, it does not say that. Paragraph 2 of article XIV states that it-
. . . shall be deemed to have come into effect on the fourteenth day of June, 1941. It shall
continue in effect for a.period of five years from that date and indefinitely after that period, but may be terminated. . . .
And so forth. It must be ratified-"shall be ratified", it says. It is binding on us the minute we ratify it.

maintopic: TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1944 CANADA-UNITED STATES OF AMERICA-RATIFICATION OF CONVENTION SIGNED AT OTTAWA, JUNE 8, 1944
speechtext: A treaty cannot be binding on one country unless it has been ratified by both.

speechtext: It is the law of Canada, unless you say otherwise. What we have done with previous treaties, I think, is to say that the treaty comes in effect as of a certain date when ratified by both the contracting parties. That is the way it ought to be drafted.

speechtext: 193. Canadian travel bureau service, $77,950.

maintopic: NATIONAL WAR SERVICES
speechtext:
This item, coming as it does in the civil appropriations for the Department of National War Services, involves what I might call one of the major peace-time industries and a very important one both from the national and from the international point of view. I refer to the tourist trade of Canada. The Canadian travel bureau service is one which, prior to the war, had functioned in a way that was generally acceptable to the people. Up to the time the war broke out, the tourist trade in Canada had assumed year by year greater and greater proportions. Encouragement was lent to it by the dominion government, the provincial governments, and in certain sections of the country by municipalities where the tourist trade was one of the major sources of revenue of the people in that particular district. During the war-

time period, of course, tourist travel had pretty well diminished to a point where only a skeleton was left of what it was in pre-war days. It was one of the war's casualties so far as peace-time activity is concerned. That was particularly the case with respect to tourists coming from the United States and other countries. The reciprocal arrangements which existed in pre-war days whereby our people went south and their people came here had to be temporarily suspended and practically abandoned.
I have found, and I think the minister has found, that as the war reaches the point where it is at least nearer to its climax, if one may put it in that way, the attention of the public begins to be focused a little more on the peacetime activities which will follow. It is essential that in any move we make so far as reconstruction or making plans for the peacetime period are concerned we never let our eye wander off the ball, so to speak, as far as the winning of the war is concerned. Yet I think there is always in the back of the minds of the people this thought. It has cost us a lot in men, money and materials because we were unprepared for war. There are many people who believe that had we been prepared for war at an earlier time perhaps there would not have been any war, but I will leave that to those who know much more about international complications than I. However, it does rest with us when this war is over-and I pray and I think we all pray that that time may not be too far distant, although most of us have fears that perhaps we are not as near that time as some would have us believe-the responsibility of making sure that the peacetime period is prepared for so that we shall not have the helter-skelter arrangements that were necessary for us to make in the preparation for this war. That responsibility rests upon the government and upon the people. The helter-skelter arrangements that we had to make in preparation for the war were not confined to this country. The whole democratic free world found itself in the same position in trying to convert its peace-time activities and enterprises into a war-time economy.
I think I shall have some corroboration and support from hon. members of the committee when I make this statement. When peace comes there will be a desire on the part of people generally to do some travelling that has been accumulating in their minds during this period of great stress and strain. I suppose there is scarcely an hon. member in this committee who has not given some thought-and he does not have very much time for leisure- to what kind of travelling he is going to do as a means of relaxation when the war is

Sup-ply-War Services
over. That, of course, is in the minds of people generally. When this war draws to its close the tourist trade no doubt will assume greater proportions in this country than ever before. I do not often indulge in prophecy, but were I so tempted I would say that the tourist industry of Canada before the war will look puny and insignificant alongside the tremendous business that this country will do when the days of peace come. This means that we must be prepared. We cannot expect to reach this period unprepared and still do our duty to our nation and to those from other lands to whom we are acting as hosts. Therefore I welcome at least the approach to the problem as is indicated by the increase in the estimates in this civil appropriation.
I am not in a position to say as to whether or not the money which has been increased by some 123,000-it seems small-is put in the right place; but in any event it does indicate that there is a consciousness on the part of the director of the Canadian travel bureau services that in the future there will be an expansion in a business which was a very important one to us in the past. When this country is making its preparations for the tourist trade I am hopeful that it will make sure that the preparations are of such a nature that they will fit into the place which we trust this nation will fill in world affairs. I am hopeful that as a nation we shall see to it that we put our best foot forward in this business. It means a lot to the people of Canada. It started out as a business which was a sort of sideline; it then developed into a business of major proportions.
When we talk about the planning for reconstruction in the years to come I think those plans will not be complete unless the reconstruction of the tourist business of Canada is fitted into that general programme. No doubt the minister of reconstruction will have a goodly share in the plans for the period that lies ahead; but I wish to point out to the minister and to the government that they ought to be in a position now to tell us something about the plans. I am going to ask the minister to describe in some detail the plans which this government have already laid out with respect to this portion of our country's reconstruction programme, because this is a programme which can be worked out quite a distance ahead. Some programmes, such as the reconversion and changing over of industries from war time to peace time, must of necessity be delayed because conditions may arise in this country which may interfere seriously and perhaps change the plans altogether. But that does not apply to the same extent to the tourist trade, because the
general basic factors I think ought now to be fairly well known to the government. It is true that there may be some influences and factors which will be changed; but the minister has received briefs from various organizations; many people have given a great deal of thought to the matter of tourist traffic after the war and what it will mean to this country, and I hope that the minister will come along with a programme for this country for the post-war years. In the details given for this item I notice that the amount for advertising and publicity has been increased this year by some $15,000, while the amount allocated for publications has been increased from $3,000 to $6,000. Other than the cost of temporary assistance I believe those are the most noticeable increases in the item.
I wish to impress upon the minister the necessity of drawing up this plan at an early day, for this is something the government can get at now. I believe the programme laid down in this connection will occupy a position of great importance as far as our national economy is concerned in the future. One of the things that will be very important in connection with the promotion and advancement of the tourist industry will be the means of transportation. I suggest to the minister that we are entering an era of air travel. Those who lived in the nineties saw the transition from horse-drawn to motor-driven vehicles. I think we who were brought up in the automobile era will live to see t'he day when automobiles will be largely displaced by aeroplanes, helicopters and other forms of air transport. So that I think it is very important that in making plans for the tourist traffic we should take into consideration the new types of conveyances that will bring people to this country. I suggest that the country most far-sighted and most advanced in getting tourists to visit it, and in providing the most comfortable and convenient forms of transportation within it, will have a great advantage over other countries in competing for this valuable business.
I suggest to the minister that we must also complete our highway system by constructing the links necessary to do away with the deadends that exist at the present time. It is a national duty and obligation to prepare in every way possible for this tourist trade. We shall have to consider our highways more than we have considered them in the past. We shall have to see that proper facilities for landing, refueling and repairing planes are provided. Let us not be caught unprepared for this new era, as we have been caught so often before, for I am sure even this government can see the development that is coming.

I am going to ask the minister, if I may, to unfold the details of the programme which I am sure the government must have in hand concerning this great business in the post-war years.

I have just a word to add in connection with the important item now under discussion. I believe the leader of the opposition is to be congratulated upon the vision he has displayed and his real grasp of the situation in regard to the task which lies ahead as far as Canada is concerned in connection with the development of our great tourist industry. The constituency I represent is particularly interested in that industry; through the hand of fate, and through an extraordinary occurrence some nine years ago, that constituency has probably had as many visitors from across the line as any other constituency in Canada, so that my people are deeply concerned with this matter. I believe the minister is to be congratulated also upon his thorough grasp of the situation, although he took over this task only a comparatively short time ago. The committee may not know that early in December of last year he called a conference in the city of Quebec to which were invited the officers in charge of the tourist industry in all nine provinces. A report of that convention was issued; I have read it from cover to cover, and it shows that not only this government but the provincial governments are awakening to the increasing importance of this industry.
There is another factor to which I might properly refer. I believe the minister is fortunate in having as director of the travel bureau Mr. Leo Dolan, who has occupied that position for some years. Hon. members may not recall that some three years ago there was a meeting in California of representatives of the United States, Canada, and the twenty-one South and Central American countries for the purpose of forming an international travel association. Canada was represented by the director of our travel bureau. At that meeting Canada was accorded the signal honour of having Mr. Dolan elected as the first president of the association, for a two-year term.

I think I am safe in saying that before the war the tourist industry in Canada was worth more to our national economy in the way of foreign exchange than our great timber operations. This comparison gives us an idea of the great importance of the tourist industry to Canada. I trust there will be no objection to my taking a few minutes to place on the record some information which I think this committee should have and which should prove of interest to the public.
The reasons for this estimate are to keep alive during the war interest in our tourist trade and to protect our heavy investments in highways, railways, bus systems, steamship lines, air lines, hotels, eating places, popular resorts, the gasoline and oil distributing trades, the tourist trade generally and foreign exchange. There is one item of great importance internationally, that of good will, and there is also the question of the nation's health in mind and body. While we want visitors to come to Canada in large numbers when circumstances will permit, I should like to see the Canadian public travel and enjoy themselves in order to keep up their morale and improve their physique and health. As soon as the invasion broke out I decided that it would not now be proper to call in these representatives, and early last month I wrote them as follows:
It had ibee.n my intention to invite the members of the national tourist advisory committee to a meeting some time in July. However, in view of the situation which has developed in Europe, it seems advisable to postpone the meeting.
Upon reflection, I hope you will agree that it is not wise to assemble the committee at this time. At this moment when the hearts and minds of Canadian people are focused upon the course of the invasion of Europe, such a meeting might not be understood. It may be that our forces in France will have dealt a crushing blow to the-enemy later in the summer. If such be the case-and God willing we all hope it will be so-it may be possible to assemble the committee late in the fall.
In the meantime it would be very much appreciated if you would care to express any thoughts you may have to Mr. D. Leo Lolan, executive director of the committee. It might be well at your convenience, if you would make known your views to Mr. Dolan as to the points you believe should be discussed by the members of the committee when they meet.
We had replies from nearly all the members of the committee. A report on the consensus of the opinion expressed in those replies reads as follows:
In connection with the letter issued by the minister, under date of June 17. to the members of the national tourist advisory committee, I beg to make the following report.
We have now received replies from practically every member of the committee. These replies indicate unanimous approval of the minister's action in not holding a meeting of the committee at the present time. Further, the members have indicated their desire to agree with the minister's proposal that we should meet late in September or October.
The leader of the opposition asked that I outline the plans for the future, and I shall do my best to satisfy him on that point. It is the opinion of many persons in Canada directly interested in the tourist trade, such as hotelkeepers, resort owners and other people in the trade, that immediately after the war is ended we shall not be relieved of the traffic rush which exists to-day and that therefore that it would be inadvisable to attempt to increase the passenger traffic. At the moment our trains are filled with passengers, and of course as far as road travel is concerned we are hampered by the scarcity of gasoline and rubber. I hope the rubber situation will be corrected very quickly, owing to the synthetic plants
that are now going very well, but gasoline is another matter. However, that is one of the things which will be in greater supply I believe as soon as the peak of the war has been reached and passed victoriously.
As to the future, I shall be. glad to send my hon. friend a copy of the report of the proceedings of the national tourist business meeting held on my invitation at the Chateau Frontenac, Quebec city, November 29 and December 1, 1943. About 250 Canadians and Americans interested directly in the tourist trade met to discuss matters of mutual interest, and I believe they were in unanimous agreement on all subjects. It was my pleasure to address the delegates and outline to them what I considered the principal features of a successful tourist trade. I invited them to give these their attention and to work along the lines I suggested. .
The committee sat and passed resolutions, which resolutions will be considered by the advisory committee when it meets. I am anxious to meet these gentlemen because they are all keenly intent upon advancing the prosperity and happiness of Canada. They appreciate the value of this industry to the national economy, and they can do an immense amount of good in creating international good feeling because many of them are hosts to many visitors who come to enjoy Canada's climate and beauty.

I am afraid I have drawn a blank so far as getting information with respect to the government's plans for the tourist industry. The minister may have overlooked that part of my question. We have now had quite a long period of inactivity so far as the Canadian travel bureau is concerned. We are now in the sixth year of the war, and during this period of relative inactivity in the tourist trade it seems to me that the government ought to have prepared some constructive programme to be placed before this committee with respect to the policy which is to be followed in the post-war period with respect to the tourist trade.
I rose to find out what plans the government has made, because there is criticism across the country to the effect that we talk a lot about reconstruction but that when it comes down to having plans ready we do not get much more from the government than statements that inquiries are being made and advisory committees are being set up. Advisory committees are all to the good and I am not intending any reflection at all on the personnel of the advisory committee. But anyone who talks to those in the tourist industry knows they are not entirely satisfied that we have proceeded far enough or vigorously enough with a tourist programme for the post-war period. Whether the minister realizes it or not-and I fancy he does-the tourist business is something that ought to occupy a major part of his attention at this time. But we seem to go blithely along talking about reconstruction in the post-war period and here is a definite part and parcel of the reconstruction programme. This is one case-perhaps there are others-where a programme should have been prepared for developing and promoting the tourist industry in this country. This committee ought to have before it now the tourist programme which the government proposes to inaugurate in the period of peace. I think I am not asking the minister too much when I ask
that. I think I am but reflecting the thoughts of a great many people engaged in the tourist industry who are not sure that there has been any more than words and talk with respect to this part of the government's activities in the reconstruction period. I do not want to seem unduly critical of the minister. What I am saying is rather a reflection of the complaints and criticisms that I have heard myself with respect to the programme or lack of a definite constructive programme with respect to the tourist industry in the postwar period.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am indebted to the hon. leader of the opposition for having spoken so frankly. In return he will not mind if I speak equally frankly. The hon. gentleman tells this committee that his words reflect the opinions that have been brought to his attention. May I tell him that I am in direct communication with the tourist trade all over this country, and I have not heard one single word or suspicion of a thought such as the leader of the opposition has expressed to-night.
The words which have been used by the leader of the opposition to describe the thoughts of those with whom he has been in contact are not what has been said to me. May I tell him that the suggestions contained in the report have been adopted and followed and applauded by the tourist trade of Canada. A moment ago I read a letter which I wrote to the advisory committee on June 17, and gave the consensus of leaders in the tourist trade in Canada, approving my suggestion and sharing my hope that we could meet in the fall. I cannot conceive that that is of the nature of the reaction described to us by the hon. leader of the opposition, because everything that I know and everything that I have heard is definitely to the contrary.
A moment ago I said that I would send to the leader of the opposition a copy of the report of the proceedings of the national tourists' business meeting which was held in Quebec last winter. May I also table a copy of that report this evening, with the consent of the committee. Before the minister answers
that question may I say that I am interested in the attitude the leader of the opposition takes with regard to this and other departments of government, when he asks them to define their post-war programmes. - I have often marvelled at the insistence with which opposition groups make this kind of demand, when in my view the formulating of plans for the post-war period is dependent upon the results of the peace conference, which in turn will depend a great deal upon who sits at that conference, the ideals which are promoted there, and how they affect the people of the various countries involved. It is unfair to insist that various ministers should state a special and particular programme. One has to face facts. You cannot mark out a blueprint which can be applied five years from now. This war is not over. We do not yet know who will sit at the peace conference, whether nationialism or internationalism will rule, whether the Atlantic charter will be implemented. One of the greatest contributions to the promotion of tourist trade prior to the war was the reciprocal arrangement for the admission of $100 worth of goods duty-free at the border, which induced millions of people from the United States to patronize our market. Behind that I stand and to that end I have worked. It will not displease the leader of the opposition to learn, perhaps for the first time, that I gathered together those who own these businesses, and therefore cannot be regimented and told what to do, except to invite them to think of the future and to be prepared for it, and to offer them assistance in carrying out the policy I read a moment ago. I think that sufficed, and perhaps all the better because nothing like it had ever been attempted before I did it. If the leader of the opposition were to read this report which I am tabling, and of which I am sending him a copy, perhaps he would realize that there is more to it than he seems to believe.

I thought this was an opportune time for me to bring to the attention of the minister a thought I had for some time. In my opinion we should be making more and more use of the national film board to educate the public in a visual manner regarding the task and function of government. Our system of government is a democratic one. That, of course premises a partnership between the people and those in public office, and the activities of government have expanded to such an extent that I am quite certain one of the real dangers to the democratic way of government is a growing apart of the people from their own government. The amounts that governments now handle, the amount of the budget and the range of activities, are so immense that the average person on the street is inclined to think of government as some agency completely apart from himself and from the things which affect his life and in which he has a vital partnership.
Government, after all, is but the agent chosen by the people to conduct their business, and I am much alarmed as I notice the chasm that separates the people's mind from the activities of government. One of the things we must do is to realize that such agencies as the national film board can interpret government to the people and help them to be fully informed of the details of different regulations and laws that affect them in their daily 
life. I often think that the many pamphlets and other forms of literature distributed do not accomplish the purpose intended. I know they are excellent in form and material, but there are'many people who have not the time or interest to peruse all the different forms of literature sent out by the various departments.
During the war some of the films produced by the national film board to bring home some lesson of war, and the practical necessity of some regulation or rule or restriction, have shown the ability of the board to present these things in a vivid manner that quickly brings to the person seeing them the purpose of some particular regulation and the manner in which it is beneficial to him as a citizen of the country. Therefore I believe in Canada that more and more must be considered and solved if we are to make democracy what it should be, a matter of close interest on the part of our people. Knowing the ability of this national film board-and I say to the minister that I highly compliment that particular board on its ability to produce in a visual form government pictures of very great interest, and, in my opinion, of very great technical skill-I think it is an agency that Canada could well be proud of. and that we should use it a great deal more than we have been doing in order to perform the national duty of interpreting Canada and its activities to the people of this country.
